profiles.name: Mubarak Hamed
profiles.description:
Mubarak Hamed was the executive director of the now-defunct Islamic American Relief Agency from 1991 to October 2004. He admitted to sending more than $1 million to Iraq in violation of U.S. sanctions.

Case characteristics: FISA surveillance. Organization referenced in charging documents: Islamic American Relief Agency.

Case data and description from The Intercept's Trial and Terror project (Trevor Aaronson and Margot Williams), licensed CC BY-NC. Source: https://github.com/theintercept/trial-and-terror-data
profiles.finding: DOJ exhibits, AP/KSL and Charity & Security Network corroborate identity; no usable subject portrait verified. Devex author image is not Hamed.

profiles.name: Marcel Johnson
profiles.description: Marcel "Khali" Johnson, a Black Occupy Oakland organizer involved in food and blanket distribution at the Frank Ogawa Plaza encampment, was arrested December 16, 2011 outside Oakland City Hall in a dispute over a blanket and anti-encroachment ordinance violations. Because of an unrelated Sacramento probation hold, he was sent to Santa Rita Jail rather than released. There he was placed in solitary confinement and denied his prescribed psychiatric medication; an altercation with a corrections officer in solitary led to a felony assault charge that, layered with two prior strikes, exposed him to a potential life sentence under California's three-strikes law. The case was prosecuted aggressively by the Alameda County DA over the objections of a robust Occupy legal-defense campaign led by attorney Dan Siegel. Johnson served approximately one year in solitary at California Men's Colony (CMC) before being transferred to California State Prison Sacramento (CSP-Sac), where he remained at least through late 2014.
profiles.finding: Daily Kos interview/video and SF Bay Guardian identify Khali as Marcel Johnson; Daily Kos retrieval failed. Oakland baseball coach not linked. Video portrait lead pending.

profiles.name: Carlos Coleman
profiles.description:
Member ("King Spanky") of the Greensboro chapter of the Almighty Latin King & Queen Nation. Indicted December 2011 in the federal RICO case against the Greensboro Latin Kings and pleaded guilty prior to the October 2012 trial.

The record of a guilty plea is incorrect: Coleman went to trial in United States v. Cornell, and on November 13, 2012, the court granted his Rule 29 motion for judgment of acquittal and dismissed the case against him. He was never convicted, and left custody with the acquittal.
profiles.finding: United States v Cornell identifies King Spanky; no verified portrait located.

profiles.name: Corey Donahue
profiles.description: Corey Donahue was one of the most-arrested figures of the entire Occupy movement, an Occupy Denver organizer cited and detained dozens of times during the Civic Center Park encampment. Most prominently he was charged in connection with a November 13, 2011 incident at the encampment with two felony counts of inciting a riot plus a misdemeanor obstruction count. Donahue eventually pleaded out via a global plea deal and served approximately 9 months at the Denver County Jail on the riot/obstruction charges (concurrent with separate misdemeanor unlawful-sexual-contact case from a March 2012 confrontation with TV journalist Eli Stokols, which complicated his support among other Occupy organizers).
profiles.finding: Westword interview corroborates Occupy Denver identity; retrieved article HTML has no usable portrait. Tampa realtor and Florida arrest namesakes not linked and rejected.

profiles.name: Cesar Aguirre
profiles.description: Cesar Aguirre, then 24 and from Elk Grove, California, was prosecuted for actions during the November 2-3, 2011 Occupy Oakland general strike. Following the strike's late-night march on the OPD Internal Affairs and Recruiting Office near Oakland City Hall, prosecutors said Aguirre struck the building's windows multiple times with a red metal folding chair, breaking six windows and a door. Convicted in mid-2012 of felony vandalism; in September 2012 sentenced to six months in the Alameda County Jail, five years probation, $6,654 in restitution, and a five-year stay-away order from Frank Ogawa Plaza. Aguirre had already served roughly four months in pretrial custody. He maintained he was innocent throughout.
profiles.finding: KQED and federal court records corroborate Occupy Oakland case; Flickr photographer, lawyer and Nicaraguan politician not linked and rejected.

profiles.name: Jesse William Waters
profiles.description: Jesse William Waters, age 30, was indicted in 2011 for his role in 1999 New Years Eve Michigan State University Agriculture Hall arson, working with Marie/Marius Mason and Frank Ambrose. Pleaded guilty to misprision; 6 months federal prison plus 1 year supervised release.
profiles.finding: Sprout Distro support page corroborates ELF identity and prisoner number. No verified portrait located.

profiles.name: Izhar Khan
profiles.description: Izhar Khan was an imam at Jamaat Al-Mu’mineen Mosque in Margate, Florida. Federal agents arrested him on May 14, 2011 with his father, Hafiz Khan, and brother, Irfan Khan, in a prosecution alleging support for the Pakistani Taliban. During trial, U.S. District Judge Robert Scola found the evidence against Izhar Khan insufficient and entered a judgment of acquittal on January 17, 2013. He was released that day after 614 days in custody.
profiles.finding: Getty release-day photo identifies imam in group. Commons image describes University of Glasgow subject, not independently linked to imam, so not used. Getty licensing and crop unresolved.

profiles.name: Hafiz Muhammad Sher Ali Khan
profiles.description: Hafiz Muhammad Sher Ali Khan was a Pakistan-born U.S. citizen and imam at Miami Masjid, also known as the Flagler Mosque. Federal agents arrested him in South Florida on May 14, 2011. After a two-month trial, a jury convicted him on March 4, 2013 of four counts involving conspiracy and material support for the Pakistani Taliban. The evidence concerned money sent to contacts and sympathizers in Pakistan. Khan maintained that the transfers supported relatives, friends, and a religious school he founded. On August 23, 2013, Judge Robert Scola sentenced him to 25 years in federal prison. A federal judge granted compassionate release on October 11, 2019 because of his advanced illnesses, and he was released to hospice care.
profiles.finding: Appellate opinion and CBS case reporting corroborate identity; no usable individual portrait verified. Florida newspaper PDF remains a lead.

profiles.name: Nachimuthu Socrates
profiles.description:
Socrates, Murugesu Vinayagamoorthy, Vijayshanthar Patpanathan, Gaspar Raj Maria Paulian, Namasivaya Viswanathan, and an unknown individual conspired to provide resources, currency, training, and false documents to the Tamil Tigers. Socrates wrote a $500 check to an informant posing as a State Department official and then gave $5,000 to another person he believed was also a State Department official. In addition, Socrates relayed to a Tamil Tigers member the contents of what he believed was a classified document purchased from State Department officials.

Case characteristics: FBI sting operation, FBI confidential informant. Organization referenced in charging documents: Tamil Tigers.

Case data and description from The Intercept's Trial and Terror project (Trevor Aaronson and Margot Williams), licensed CC BY-NC. Source: https://github.com/theintercept/trial-and-terror-data

profiles.name: Brian Thomas Mettenbrink
profiles.description: Brian Thomas Mettenbrink is an Anonymous hacktivist who was charged as part of a group who conducted a DDoS attack on the Church of Scientology's websites. He plead guilty and was sentenced to one year in prison.
profiles.finding: DOJ confirms case. We Are Legion documentary interview is potential portrait lead; current news images not verified as subject. No portrait added.

profiles.name: Cailin Elizabeth Major
profiles.description: Cailin Elizabeth Major, then 25 and living in Milwaukee, was arrested after the May 1, 2010 anti-capitalist May Day demonstration in downtown Asheville, North Carolina. Major was among eleven defendants charged in connection with property damage during the demonstration. She was released on bond on May 5, 2010. Prosecutors later dismissed the charges without leave.
profiles.finding: Denver ABC Asheville list and Bash Back court materials corroborate name; no verified portrait located.
